## Introduction

The aim of this notebook is to use MaxEnt to estimate how climate change will impact the habitat of *Eucalyptus pauciflora subsp. niphophila* for use in an ECBA submission.

The specific criteria being addressed is:

> *2b) **Continuing decline** observed, estimated, inferred or **projected** in any of: (i) extent of occurrence; (ii) area of occupancy; **(iii) area, extent and/or quality of habitat;** (iv) number of locations or subpopulations; (v) number of mature individuals."*

That is, we're trying to quantify the decline in the area of *niphophila* habitat under future climate change projections.

### Some similar analyses

- Ren, Jun, Suhang Li, Yawen Zhang, Qiong Yang, Jiaojiao Liu, Jing Fan, and Yangzhou Xiang. 2025. ‘MaxEnt-Based Evaluation of Climate Change Effects on the Habitat Suitability of Magnolia Officinalis in China’. *Frontiers in Plant Science* 16:1601585. doi:[10.3389/fpls.2025.1601585](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2025.1601585).

### Useful references for MaxEnt modeling:

- Merow, C., Smith, M. J., & Silander, J. A. (2013). A practical guide to MaxEnt for modeling species’ distributions: What it does, and why inputs and settings matter. Ecography, 36(10), 1058–1069. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1600-0587.2013.07872.x
- Elith, J., Phillips, S. J., Hastie, T., Dudík, M., Chee, Y. E., & Yates, C. J. (2011). A statistical explanation of MaxEnt for ecologists: Statistical explanation of MaxEnt. Diversity and Distributions, 17(1), 43–57. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1472-4642.2010.00725.x

## Prepare observational data

### Download the occurrence data

The first thing I'll do is import the *E. niphophila* observational data. I'm using the `galah` package, which lets me access all of the data compiled by the Atlas of Living Australia (ALA). Observations come from a number of sources such as government agencies (mostly DEECCEW, herbaria, and iNaturalist.

I'm going to download just about every column that could possibly be of use, including a bunch of built-in data quality checks which we can use to exclude low quality observations from the training data.

- [Descriptions of the data quality variables](https://github.com/AtlasOfLivingAustralia/ala-dataquality/wiki)

- [Descriptions of the environmental variables](https://biocache.ala.org.au/fields?filter=name%3Ael%5B0-9%5D*&max=100&order=DESC&sort=classs)

```{r}
# If niph_raw has already been downloaded, import it. Otherwise, download observations from
# the Atlas of Living Australia, including >100 metadata columns.

niph_raw_path <- here::here("data/galah/niph_raw.rds")

if (file.exists(niph_raw_path)) {
  
  niph_raw <- readr::read_rds(niph_raw_path)
  
} else {
  
  # Construct an API call to galah. Some columns can be accessed in predefined groups
  
  niph_raw_call <- galah_call() |>
    identify("Eucalyptus pauciflora subsp. niphophila") |>
    select(
      group = c(
        "basic", # record_id, lat/lon, etc.
        "event", # columns describing the observation process
        "assertions" # data quality checks
      ),
      starts_with("el"), # environmental variables
      "coordinateUncertaintyInMeters",
      "spatiallyValid",
      "isDuplicateOf",
      "outlierLayerCount",
      "year",
      "country",
      "stateProvince",
      "identifiedBy",
      "locality",
      "institutionCode"
    )
  
  # Download our occurrence data
  
  niph_raw <- atlas_occurrences(niph_raw_call)
  
  # Save the raw data as an rds file
  
  readr::write_rds(niph_raw, niph_raw_path)
}

cat("Number of unfiltered Niphophila observations: ", nrow(niph_raw))
```

### Filter out low-quality data

Not all of this data is super high quality, so we can apply some data quality filters to try and filter out unreliable records. I'm basing this on the data quality filters ALA suggests for species distribution modelling, along with some additional data quality checks.

The most important data quality filters are

- [`spatiallyValid`](https://github.com/AtlasOfLivingAustralia/ala-dataquality/wiki/spatiallyValid)`== TRUE`: Built-in checks to make sure the coordinates are valid and logically consistent

- [`is.na(isDuplicateOf)`](https://github.com/AtlasOfLivingAustralia/ala-dataquality/wiki/isDuplicateOf): The record hasn't been flagged by ALA as a duplicate

- [`outlierLayerCount`](https://github.com/AtlasOfLivingAustralia/ala-dataquality/wiki/outlierLayerCount)`== 0`: The record hasn't been flagged by ALA as an outlier when compared with other environmental data.

- [`coordinateUncertaintyInMeters`](https://github.com/AtlasOfLivingAustralia/ala-dataquality/wiki/coordinate_uncertainty)`<= 1000`: Estimated coordinate uncertainty is less than 1 km. Records with no uncertainty estimate are removed as well.

- I'm also removing records from before 1970, or which aren't in NSW, ACT, or Victoria.

```{r}
# Apply data quality checks

niph_raw_filtered <- niph_raw |> 
  filter(
    occurrenceStatus == "PRESENT", # Not actually necessary, but reassuring
    !is.na(decimalLongitude), 
    !is.na(decimalLatitude),
    coordinateUncertaintyInMeters <= 1000,
    spatiallyValid == TRUE,
    is.na(isDuplicateOf),
    outlierLayerCount == 0,
    year >= 1970,
    country == "Australia",
    stateProvince %in% c("Victoria", "Australian Capital Territory", "New South Wales")
  )

# Select a more readable subset of columns to use in the rest of the analysis

niph_filtered <- niph_raw_filtered |>
  select(
    "recordID",
    "scientificName",
    "decimalLongitude",
    "decimalLatitude",
    "coordinateUncertaintyInMeters",
    "eventDate",
    "year",
    "basisOfRecord",
    "identifiedBy",
    "locality",
    "stateProvince",
    "dataResourceName",
    "institutionCode"
  )

# Convert the observations into a spatial object

niph_filtered_sf <- st_as_sf(
  niph_filtered, 
  coords = c("decimalLongitude", "decimalLatitude"), 
  crs = crs_geog
)

# View the records in an interactive map

mapview(niph_filtered_sf)
```

### Targeted outlier removal

Some observations are still suspicious, despite passing the data quality checks. I'll remove these records explicitly.

+--------------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| **recordID**                         | **Reason for removal**                                                                  |
+======================================+=========================================================================================+
| 2c4dd780-74ef-4337-893b-250e47aa64a8 | In Grampians NP, well outside known range                                               |
+--------------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| f1047be9-66f7-4ba6-9157-d0f1d906fa12 | In Baw Baw NP and from 1994, so likely to be the Baw Baw subspecies (described in 1994) |
|                                      |                                                                                         |
| 56c4cb9d-db98-4f0c-8080-d75a281a5b06 |                                                                                         |
+--------------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

```{r}
suspicious_records <- c(
  "2c4dd780-74ef-4337-893b-250e47aa64a8",
  "f1047be9-66f7-4ba6-9157-d0f1d906fa12",
  "56c4cb9d-db98-4f0c-8080-d75a281a5b06"
)

niph_notsus_sf <- niph_filtered_sf |> 
  filter(
    recordID %notin% suspicious_records
  )

niph_filtered_sf |> 
  mutate(suspicious = recordID %in% suspicious_records) |> 
  mapview(zcol = "suspicious")
```

### Check the elevations

*Niphophila* is known to inhabit altitudes above 1600 m. To allow for some natural variation we'll allow records down to 1400 m, but any records below this altitude will be removed as they have a higher likelihood of being misidentified.

```{r}
# Download a 5 degree tile of 3s elevation data which covers the observations.
# 3s data is on a grid of around 90 m x 90 m, which is more accurate than most of our data.

elev_3s <- geodata::elevation_3s(lon = 147.5, lat = -37.5, path = here::here("data"))

# Convert our observations to SpatVector to work with the terra package

niph_vect <- vect(niph_notsus_sf)

# Extract the elevation at each point

niph_elevs <- extract(elev_3s, niph_vect)

# Construct a buffer around each observation to account for positional uncertainty

niph_buffers <- buffer(
  niph_vect, 
  width = niph_notsus_sf$coordinateUncertaintyInMeters
)

# Extract the maximum and minimum elevations in each buffer zone

niph_elev_ranges <- extract(elev_3s, niph_buffers, fun = range, na.rm = TRUE)

# Join the extracted elevation data back to our raw data set

niph_elev_sf <- niph_notsus_sf |>
  mutate(
    elevation_m = niph_elevs[[2]],
    elevation_m_min = niph_elev_ranges[, 2],
    elevation_m_max = niph_elev_ranges[, 3]
  )

# Filter out records below 1400 m

niph_elev_filter_sf <- niph_elev_sf |> 
  filter(elevation_m >= 1400)

# Have a look at the observations we just filtered out

niph_elev_sf |> 
  mutate(below_alt = elevation_m < 1400) |> 
  mapview(zcol = "below_alt", alpha.regions = 0.8)
```

### Australian Alps bioregion

The Australian Alps bioregion will form the foundation of our study area definition. I'll also use it to exclude any final records which might not be where we expect to find *Niphophila*.

```{r}
# The bioregions geodatabase doesn't download automatically. If needed, download it from
# https://fed.dcceew.gov.au/datasets/interim-biogeographic-regionalisation-for-australia-ibra-version-7-1-regions/about

# Import the Australian Alps bioregion polygon

aus_alps <- st_read(here::here("data/IBRA7_regions.gdb")) |>
  filter(REG_NAME_7 == "Australian Alps") |> 
  st_transform(4326) |> 
  st_union()

# Identify any observations outside the bioregion

niph_outside_aus_alps <- niph_elev_filter_sf |> 
  st_filter(aus_alps, .predicate = st_disjoint)

# Plot just the points outside the bioregion

mapview(aus_alps, alpha.regions = 0.5, lwd = 2, alpha = 1) +
  mapview(niph_outside_aus_alps, col.regions = "red")
```

There are three observations outside the bioregion, all clustered around Thredbo and all very close to the region. Let's look see exactly how far they are from the bioregon.

```{r}
niph_outside_aus_alps |>
  as_tibble() |> 
  mutate(dist_to_bioregion = st_distance(niph_outside_aus_alps, aus_alps)[, 1]) |> 
  select(
    dist_to_bioregion,
    coordinateUncertaintyInMeters, 
    elevation_m,
    elevation_m_min,
    elevation_m_max
  )
```

Okay, so they're all within 100 m of the bioregion, which is within the bounds of their positional uncertainty. As there is also some inaccuracy in the bioregion definition I'm inclined to keep them in the data set - excluding them would be arbitrary.

## Define the study area

The study area is the region of environmental conditions we're interesting in contrasting our presence values against, i.e. places *Niphophila* could have reached and been recorded. We also need to include area beyond this range to give the model something to compare against.

I'll be basing the study area on the Australian Alps bioregion. All of our observations are within or very close to this area, however some parts of the bioregion have no observations and so either haven't been surveyed or aren't candidates for dispersal. As such, I'll remove any polygons which don't have an observation within 1 km.

```{r}
# To look at distances between points we need to move to a projected CRS

niph_proj <- niph_sf |> 
  st_transform(crs_proj)

aus_alps_proj <- aus_alps |> 
  st_transform(crs_proj) |> 
  st_cast("POLYGON")

# Check if our points are within 1000 m of an observation

within_dist <- lengths(st_is_within_distance(aus_alps_proj, niph_proj, dist = 1000)) > 0

aus_alps_parts <- st_sf(geometry = aus_alps_proj) |> 
  mutate(keep = within_dist)

mapview(aus_alps_parts, zcol = "keep") +
  mapview(niph_proj, col.regions = "purple")
```

To finish creating the study area I'll add a small buffer around the remaining polygons. This accounts for uncertainty in the bioregion definition.

```{r}
study_area <- aus_alps_parts |> 
  filter(keep) |> 
  st_union() |> 
  st_buffer(dist = 100, joinStyle = "MITRE", mitreLimit = 2) |> 
  smoothr::fill_holes(units::set_units(1, km^2)) |> 
  smoothr::smooth(method = "ksmooth", smoothness = 2) |> 
  st_transform(crs_geog) |> 
  st_make_valid()

mapview(study_area, alpha.regions = 0.3, lwd = 2, alpha = 1) +
  mapview(niph_sf, col.regions = "purple")
```

There are still parts of the study area which don't have any observations. Possibly these should be removed. Alternatively, multiple different study areas can be tested to see if it effects the output.

```{r}
# Double check that all observations are within the study area (expect 0 rows)

st_filter(niph_sf, study_area, .predicate = st_disjoint) |> 
  nrow()
```

Let's have a look at the elevation distribution in our study area.

```{r}
study_area_elev <- elev_3s |>
  crop(vect(study_area)) |>
  mask(vect(study_area))

plot(study_area_elev)
```

```{r}
hist(study_area_elev, breaks = 50, maxcell = ncell(study_area_elev))
```

A large portion of our study area is below the 1400 m elevation threshold. I think this is good as it gives us information on non-habitat.

## Prepare current climate data

### Download current climate data

We can download gridded climate data from [WorldClim](https://www.worldclim.org/) at 30 second resolution (\~1 km² grid cells). This data has been averaged over the period 1970-2000.

```{r}
# WorldClim climate data is stored as 30x30 degree tiles. 
# Luckily, we only need one tile to cover the study area

clim_tile <- geodata::worldclim_tile(
  var = "bio",
  res = "0.5", # 0.5 minute resolution
  lon = 135,
  lat = -45,
  path = here::here("data")
)

# Crop the climate data to our study area, making sure that any grid cell 
# that touches the study area is included

study_area_vect <- vect(study_area)

clim <- clim_tile |>
  crop(study_area_vect, snap = "out") |>
  mask(study_area_vect, touches = TRUE)

# Create a key for interpreting the layer names

bio_names <- c(
  bio_1  = "Annual mean temp (°C)",
  bio_2  = "Mean diurnal range (°C)",
  bio_3  = "Isothermality (%)",
  bio_4  = "Temp seasonality (SD × 100)",
  bio_5  = "Max temp warmest month (°C)",
  bio_6  = "Min temp coldest month (°C)",
  bio_7  = "Temp annual range (°C)",
  bio_8  = "Mean temp wettest quarter (°C)",
  bio_9  = "Mean temp driest quarter (°C)",
  bio_10 = "Mean temp warmest quarter (°C)",
  bio_11 = "Mean temp coldest quarter (°C)",
  bio_12 = "Annual precipitation (mm)",
  bio_13 = "Precip wettest month (mm)",
  bio_14 = "Precip driest month (mm)",
  bio_15 = "Precip seasonality (CV)",
  bio_16 = "Precip wettest quarter (mm)",
  bio_17 = "Precip driest quarter (mm)",
  bio_18 = "Precip warmest quarter (mm)",
  bio_19 = "Precip coldest quarter (mm)"
)

# Plot a selection of environmental variables

plot_vars <- c("bio_1", "bio_2", "bio_5", "bio_6", "bio_7", "bio_12")

plot(clim[[plot_vars]], main = bio_names[plot_vars])
```

### Predictor selection

Many of these environmental variables are highly co-linear (they are all derived from monthly precipitation and temperature), and including all of them can cause model instability and make it difficult to assess the actual importance of each variable.

We can see this if we create a correlation plot.

```{r}
clim_corr <- layerCor(clim, "pearson", na.rm = TRUE)$correlation

corrplot::corrplot(
  clim_corr,
  method = "circle", 
  type = "upper",
  tl.col = "black"
  )
```

To deal with this, we can refine our variables down into a more meaningful set of predictors.

The four 'interactive' variables (bio_8, bio_9, bio_18, bio_19) combine information about both temperature and precipitation, and are known to have non-physical discontinuities due to variation in which quarter is wettest or warmest. These are easy candidates for removal.

To narrow down the rest of the variables we can use the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF):

1.  Regress each variable against all other variables and get an $R^2$ which is a measure of the variable's variation that can't be explained by other variables.
2.  Calculate $VIF = 1 / (1-R^2)$.
3.  If the highest VIF is above a threshold (e.g 10) remove that variable.
4.  Recalculate the VIF for the remaining variables (which will have changed).
5.  Repeat until every VIF is below the threshold.

In practice this is implemented by `usdm::vifstep`.

```{r}
# First, remove the interactive variables

interactive_vars <- c("bio_8", "bio_9", "bio_18", "bio_19")

clim_candidates <- clim[[setdiff(names(clim), interactive_vars)]]

# Then do the VIF analysis

vif_threshold <- 10

vif_exclusions <- usdm::vifstep(clim_candidates, th = vif_threshold) 

#clim_selected <- usdm::exclude(clim_candidates, vif_exclusions)

vif_exclusions
```

Using the VIF analysis we've lost bio_6, minimum temperature of the coldest month. It's probably accounted for by bio_1, bio_3, and bio_4 however I kind of want bio_6 in as it captures things like frost and snow. The correlation between bio_14 and bio_1 is also higher than I'd like (-0.87)

So, I'll run the VIF analysis again but forcing bio_6 to be included.

```{r}
vif_exclusions2 <- usdm::vifstep(clim_candidates, th = vif_threshold, keep = "bio_6") 

vif_exclusions2
```

In this set bio_6 (minimum temperature of the coldest month) has been exchanged for bio_1 (annual mean temperature). I think this is probably for the best as minimum temperatures are going to be more important for snowgums. The maximum correlation between any two variables has also been reduced, though at -0.72 it's still quite high.

```{r}
clim_selected <- usdm::exclude(clim_candidates, vif_exclusions2)

plot(clim_selected, main = bio_names[names(clim_selected)])
```

### Environmental similarity analysis

Let's see how the landscape varies with respect to the areas around our occurrence points. To do this we can construct a Multivariate Environmental Similarity Surface (MESS). This involves calculating a similarity score for each variable and each cell when compared with our observations. The MESS value is the most dissimilar score across all variables.

```{r}
# We'll do the MESS analysis using our selected variables

mess_vars <- names(clim_selected)

mess_area <- crop(clim_tile[[mess_vars]], ext(145.5, 152, -38, -35))

# Extract the climatic variables at each observation

occs_z <- terra::extract(mess_area, niph_vect, ID = FALSE) |>
  drop_na()

# Get the MESS values across the full tile (not just the study area)

occs_mess <- predicts::mess(mess_area, occs_z, full = TRUE)

# Construct a MESS plot, overlayed with our study area

plot(occs_mess[["mess"]], col = hcl.colors(100, "RdBu"), main = "Environmental similarity")
plot(study_area_vect, border = "black", lwd = 1, add = TRUE)
```

And another version where the similarity has been binned so it's a bit easier to interpret.

```{r}
# Define breaks and colours

breaks <- c(-Inf, -50, -20, -10, 0, 10, 20, 50, 100)
colours <- hcl.colors(length(brks) - 1, "RdBu")

plot(occs_mess[["mess"]], breaks = breaks, col = colours, main = "Environmental similarity")
plot(study_area_vect, border = "black", lwd = 1, add = TRUE)
```

Okay, looking pretty good then. Our study area captures all of the core habitat areas and there aren't any areas with a highly similar environment outside of our study area. There are some large chunks of our study area that have close to zero similarity, however there's not much that's actually dissimilar.

Let's actually calculate how much of the study area is dissimilar.

```{r}
# Extract the MESS values in the study area

stud_area_mess <- mask(crop(occs_mess, study_area_vect), study_area_vect)

# Find the proporation of negative MESS values

100 * global(sa_mess < 0, "mean", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]
```

So 14% of our study area is dissimilar to our observations, which seems acceptable.

We can also see which variables are driving the dissimilarity.

```{r}
# Find the index of the most dissimilar variable in each cell

most_dissimilar <- which.min(occs_mess)
levels(most_dissimilar) <- data.frame(id = seq_along(mess_vars), var = mess_vars)

# Mask cells which are already similar

most_dissimilar_masked <- mask(most_dissimilar, occs_mess[["mess"]] < 0, maskvalues = FALSE)

# Plot

plot(most_dissimilar_masked, 
     col = hcl.colors(length(mess_vars), "Set 2"),
     main = "Most dissimilar variable (MESS < 0)")
plot(study_area_vect, add = TRUE, lwd = .5)
```

Interestingly, different variables drive dissimilarity in different areas.

```{r}
plot(occs_mess, col = colours, breaks = breaks)
```

Bio_15 is basically always positive, so may not have much predictive power. This tracks with it rarely being the most dissimilar variable.

# THE REST

### Download future climate projections

We can download future climate projections from WorldClim's CMIP6 downscaled data. This matches the grid of our baseline climate date.

WorldClim gives us data at four time periods (2021-2040, 2041-2060, 2061-2080, and 2081-2100) across four Shared Socio-economic Pathways (SSPs).

Shared Socio-economic Pathways (SSP):

| Name | AR6 Emissions Label | Narrative | Warming by 2100 (°C) |
|----|----|----|----|
| SSP1-2.6 | Low | Sustainability | 1.8 |
| SSP2-4.5 | Intermediate | Middle of the road | 2.7 |
| SSP3-7.0 | High | Regional rivalry | 3.6 |
| SSP5-8.5 | Very high | Fossil-fuelled development | 4.4 |

Rather than a single climate model, we use a spread of CMIP6 GCMs (Global Climate Models) so we can later assess how much projected habitat change depends on the choice of model. WorldClim has 26 CMIP6 GCMs which is frankly too many for our purposes. If we were to use all of them we would also be introducing a new source of bias as the models are not spread evenly over the scope of possible future climatic conditions (CMIP6 had the 'hot model' problem).

We can narrow down the list of GCMs by looking at how they vary across key variables. We want to select an ensemble of \~5 models which represent a spread of possible futures whilst avoiding actual outliers.

To start with, I'll download a single tile of data for each GCM and look at how precipitation and temperature vary into the future.

```{r}
# The scenario and period we're using for testing

test_scenario <- "245"
test_period <- "2061-2080"

# List all GCM candidates. 
# The ones which have been commented out don't have data for all scenario/year combinations

gcm_candidates <- c(
  "ACCESS-CM2",
  "ACCESS-ESM1-5",
  "AWI-CM-1-1-MR",
  "BCC-CSM2-MR",
  "CanESM5",
  "CanESM5-CanOE",
  "CMCC-ESM2",
  "CNRM-CM6-1",
  "CNRM-CM6-1-HR",
  "CNRM-ESM2-1",
  "EC-Earth3-Veg",
  "EC-Earth3-Veg-LR",
  #"FIO-ESM-2-0", # Unavailable
  #"GFDL-ESM4",
  "GISS-E2-1-G",
  "GISS-E2-1-H",
  #"HadGEM3-GC31-LL",
  "INM-CM4-8",
  "INM-CM5-0",
  "IPSL-CM6A-LR",
  "MIROC6",
  "MIROC-ES2L",
  "MPI-ESM1-2-HR",
  "MPI-ESM1-2-LR",
  "MRI-ESM2-0",
  "UKESM1-0-LL"
)

# Extract the currnet mean values across our study area

bio_vars <- paste0("bio_", 1:19)

current <- global(clim[[bio_vars]], "mean", na.rm = TRUE)$mean

# Loop over all candidate gcms and calculate the mean value of each variable
# across the study area

results <- list()

for (gcm in gcm_candidates) {
  
  # Download/import the tile of data
  
  tile <- cmip6_tile(
    lon = 135,
    lat = -45,
    model = gcm,
    ssp = test_scenario,
    time = test_period,
    var = "bio",
    path = here::here("data")
  )
  
  names(tile) <- bio_vars
  
  # Crop to the study area
  
  tile <- crop(tile, study_area_vect, snap = "out")
  tile <- mask(tile, study_area_vect, touches = TRUE)
  
  # Calculate the means
  
  means <- global(tile, "mean", na.rm = TRUE)$mean
  
  # Create a tibble of the results and save it to the results list
  
  results[[gcm]] <- tibble(gcm, var = bio_vars, current, future = means)
}

# Combine the list of results into a single tibble and calculate changes compared
# with current values

gcm_change <- bind_rows(results) |>
  mutate(
    change = future - current,
    change_pct = 100 * change / current,
  )

gcm_change
```

We can now look at how these variables change into the future for each GCM.

```{r}
# Define a plotting helper to plot variable pairs

plot_spread <- function(x, y, title = NULL) {
  gcm_vars <- gcm_change |>
    # Use percent change for precip variables
    mutate(change_plot = if_else(
      var %in% paste0("bio_", 12:19), 
      change_pct, 
      change
    )) |> 
    select(gcm, var, change_plot) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = var, values_from = change_plot)
  
  gcm_vars |>
    ggplot(aes(.data[[x]], .data[[y]], label = gcm)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
    geom_point() +
    ggrepel::geom_text_repel(size = 3) +
    labs(
      x = paste("Change in", bio_names[x]),
      y = paste("Change in", bio_names[y]),
      title = title
    )
}

plot_spread("bio_6", "bio_14", "GCM spread over study area, SSP2-4.5, 2061–2080")
```

There's a few strategies we can use to narrow down this list:

- We we only need one model from each family as they will tend to produce similar results (e.g. CanESM5 and CanESM5-CanOE).

- We can exclude the models which are known to run hot or cool when compared with observations.

- We can prioritise the ACCESS models as they were developed with the Australian climate in mind.

- And finally, we can look at the models which we have left and choose the ones which give us a spread of conditions across key variables.

```{r}
# GCMs chosen to span a range of climate sensitivity (cooler to hotter projections)
future_gcms <- c("MIROC6", "MPI-ESM1-2-HR", "IPSL-CM6A-LR", "ACCESS-CM2")

# All four SSPs (emissions scenarios) available from WorldClim's CMIP6 data:
# SSP1-2.6 (low), SSP2-4.5 (moderate), SSP3-7.0 (high), SSP5-8.5 (very high)
future_ssps <- c("126", "245", "370", "585")

# Now-, near-, mid-, and long-term projections
future_time <- c("2021-2040", "2041-2060", "2061-2080", "2081-2100")

future_scenarios <- expand.grid(
  gcm = future_gcms,
  ssp = future_ssps,
  time = future_time,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Download each GCM/SSP/time tile (same tile as the current-climate download
# above), crop to the study area, and subset to the same VIF-selected predictors
future_clim <- pmap(future_scenarios, function(gcm, ssp, time) {
  clim_future_tile <- geodata::cmip6_tile(
    lon = 135,
    lat = -45,
    model = gcm,
    ssp = ssp,
    time = time,
    var = "bio",
    path = here::here("data")
  )

  # cmip6_tile() returns the same 19 bioclim variables, in the same order,
  # as worldclim_tile() above - reuse those names so we can subset by the
  # VIF-selected predictor names
  names(clim_future_tile) <- names(clim)

  crop(clim_future_tile, vect(study_area), mask = TRUE)[[names(clim_selected)]]
})

names(future_clim) <- paste(future_scenarios$gcm, future_scenarios$ssp, future_scenarios$time, sep = "_")

# Spot-check one scenario
mapview(future_clim[[1]]$bio_3)
```

### Notes

- This downloads 48 tiles (4 GCMs x 4 SSPs x 3 time periods) at the same resolution/extent as the current-climate tile, rather than 48 global rasters. Each tile is \~80 MB, so expect \~3.8 GB total (some of this may already be cached from earlier runs)

- Worth double-checking that `names(clim_future_tile) <- names(clim)` is a safe assumption - it relies on both tiles containing the same 19 bioclim variables in the same order, which should hold but hasn't been explicitly verified

- The two \~6 GB `cmip6_world()` files downloaded earlier aren't used by this version of the code and can be deleted if you want to reclaim the disk space

## Spatial thinning

To some extent, our observations are biased towards where people look rather than how *Niphophila* are actually distributed. Some observations are also clustered closely together, and if we included all of them certain environments would be overrepresented.

The standard way to get around these biases is through the process of spatial thinning. We'll do this by removing records until no two are closer than a chosen distance, e.g. 1 km. The `spThin` package repeats this process many times and selects the output that lets us keep the most data points.

### Troubling transects

Before we can thin our whole data set, we need to deal with the transects in NSW. These observations are highly spatially correlated, and will create a bias towards certain conditions. On the other hand, they are likely to be some of our best data in rarely-visited locations, so we shouldn't throw them away completely.

```{r}
# Filter out transects
```

We can define a plausible habitat area using a combination of the Australian Alps bioregion and elevation data.

Let's have a look at the elevations in the Australian Alps bioregion.

```{r}
aus_alps_elev <- elev_3s |>
  crop(vect(aus_alps)) |>
  mask(vect(aus_alps))

hist(aus_alps_elev, breaks = 50, maxcell = ncell(aus_alps_elev))
```

Okay, so there are quite a few cells where the elevation in the bioregion is well below our 1400 m limit. We can refine our study area by removing these areas.

```{r}
study_area <- aus_alps_1400 <- ifel(aus_alps_elev >= 1400, 1, NA) |> 
  as.polygons() |> 
  st_as_sf() |> 
  st_transform(7855) |>  # GDA2020 / MGA Zone 55
  smoothr::drop_crumbs(units::set_units(0.5, km^2)) |> 
  smoothr::fill_holes(units::set_units(1, km^2)) |> 
  smoothr::smooth(method = "ksmooth", smoothness = 2) |> 
  #st_buffer(300) |> 
  st_transform(4326)

# Check to see if any points have fallen outside
outside <- niph |> 
  st_transform(7855) |> 
  st_filter(study_area, .predicate = st_disjoint)

# Plot just the points outside the bioregion

mapview(study_area, alpha.regions = 0.5, lwd = 2, alpha = 1) +
  mapview(niph, col.regions = "red")
```

```{r}
study_area_elev <- elev_3s |>
  crop(vect(study_area)) |>
  mask(vect(study_area))

hist(study_area_elev, breaks = 50, maxcell = ncell(study_area_elev))
```

```{r}
# Import IBRA Bioregions Version 7.1, and select the Australian Alps bioregion
# https://fed.dcceew.gov.au/datasets/interim-biogeographic-regionalisation-for-australia-ibra-version-7-1-regions/about

# Download 30s elevation data for Australia - tiles match the climate variables

  st_as_sf() |>
```

## Spatial thinning

```{r}
# thin() wants plain lon/lat columns, not an sf geometry column
niph_coords <- niph_elev |> 
  st_transform(4326) |> 
  mutate(
    Longitude = st_coordinates(geometry)[, 1],
    Latitude = st_coordinates(geometry)[, 2],
    species = "niphophila" # spec.col is required even for a single species
  ) |> 
  st_drop_geometry()

thinned <- spThin::thin(
  loc.data = niph_coords,
  lat.col = "Latitude",
  long.col = "Longitude",
  spec.col = "species",
  thin.par = 1, # Thinning distance 1 km, should be similar to cell size
  reps = 100,
  locs.thinned.list.return = TRUE,
  write.files = FALSE,
  write.log.file = FALSE
)

# Keep the dataframe with the most retained records
best_rep <- thinned[[which.max(sapply(thinned, nrow))]]

# Re-join back to the full occurrence data to recover all original columns
niph_thinned <- niph_coords |> 
  semi_join(best_rep, by = c("Longitude", "Latitude")) |> 
  st_as_sf(coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326)

mapview(niph_thinned)
```

## Download climate data

We can download climate data from [WorldClim](https://www.worldclim.org/) at 30 second resolution (\~1 km² grid cells).

```{r}
# WorldClim climate data is stored as 30x30 degree tiles. 
# We only need one tile to cover the study area
clim_tile <- worldclim_tile(
  var = "bio",
  res = "0.5", # 0.5 minute resolution
  lon = 135,
  lat = -45,
  path = here::here("data")
)

# Crop the climate data to our study area
clim <- crop(clim_tile, vect(study_area), mask = TRUE)

# Create a key for interpreting the layer names
bioclim_names <- c(
  bio_1  = "Annual Mean Temperature",
  bio_2  = "Mean Diurnal Range",
  bio_3  = "Isothermality",
  bio_4  = "Temperature Seasonality",
  bio_5  = "Max Temperature of Warmest Month",
  bio_6  = "Min Temperature of Coldest Month",
  bio_7  = "Temperature Annual Range",
  bio_8  = "Mean Temperature of Wettest Quarter",
  bio_9  = "Mean Temperature of Driest Quarter",
  bio_10 = "Mean Temperature of Warmest Quarter",
  bio_11 = "Mean Temperature of Coldest Quarter",
  bio_12 = "Annual Precipitation",
  bio_13 = "Precipitation of Wettest Month",
  bio_14 = "Precipitation of Driest Month",
  bio_15 = "Precipitation Seasonality",
  bio_16 = "Precipitation of Wettest Quarter",
  bio_17 = "Precipitation of Driest Quarter",
  bio_18 = "Precipitation of Warmest Quarter",
  bio_19 = "Precipitation of Coldest Quarter"
)

# Plot the first variable - annual mean temperature
mapview(clim$bio_1)
```

## Select predictor variables

Many of these predictor variables are highly co-linear (e.g. Precipitation of Wettest Month and Precipitation of Wettest Quater), and including all of them can cause model instability and make it difficult to assess the importance of each variable.

```{r}
# Generate random background points across the study area
bg_points <- st_sample(study_area, size = 10000, type = "random")

# Extract climate values at these points
clim_vals <- extract(clim, vect(bg_points), ID = FALSE) |> 
  na.omit()

# Calculate a correlation matrix of the variables across our study area
cor_matrix <- cor(clim_vals, method = "pearson")

# For visual inspection of correlations
corrplot::corrplot(cor_matrix, method = "circle", type = "upper")
```

We can use the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) to remove highly correlated predictors.

```{r}
# Remove the four 'interactive' variables which are related to both temperature 
# and precipitation. These variables can have biologically meaningless discontinuities due to
# variation in which quarter counts as wettest or warmest.

interactive_vars <- c("bio_8", "bio_9", "bio_18", "bio_19")

clim_candidates <- clim[[setdiff(names(clim), interactive_vars)]]

# Iteratively remove highly correlated variables using VIF
# th = 10 is a common threshold; th = 5 is stricter
v <- usdm::vifstep(clim_candidates, th = 10, keep = "bio_6") 

clim_selected <- usdm::exclude(clim_candidates, v)

v
```

### Notes

- The decision to use 10,000 background points is totally arbitrary and should probably be justified

- The correlation between two variables being over 0.7 is still quite high

## Fit the current-climate model

We can use `ENMeval` to tune the model's feature classes and regularisation multiplier via spatial cross-validation, rather than picking these settings arbitrarily.

```{r}
# ENMevaluate() wants plain coordinate data frames, not sf objects
occs <- niph_thinned |>
  st_coordinates() |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rename(longitude = X, latitude = Y)

bg <- bg_points |>
  st_coordinates() |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rename(longitude = X, latitude = Y)

# ENMevaluate() is slow to re-run every time, so cache the result. Delete the
# cache file (or the object below) to force a re-run after upstream changes
# (e.g. to occs, bg, clim_selected, or the tuning settings)
enmeval_results_path <- here::here("data/enmeval_results.rds")

if (file.exists(enmeval_results_path)) {
  enmeval_results <- readr::read_rds(enmeval_results_path)
} else {
  # Tune feature classes (L = linear, Q = quadratic, H = hinge, P = product) and
  # regularisation multiplier, using spatial block partitioning - appropriate
  # here since occurrences are geographically clustered rather than independent
  enmeval_results <- ENMevaluate(
    occs = occs,
    envs = clim_selected,
    bg = bg,
    tune.args = list(fc = c("L", "LQ", "LQH", "LQHP"), rm = seq(0.5, 4, 0.5)),
    partitions = "block",
    algorithm = "maxnet"
  )

  readr::write_rds(enmeval_results, enmeval_results_path)
}

# Inspect tuning results, ranked by AICc (lower = better fit/complexity trade-off)
enmeval_results@results |>
  arrange(AICc)
```

```{r}
# Select the best-supported settings (lowest AICc) and pull out that model
best_settings <- enmeval_results@results |>
  filter(delta.AICc == 0)

maxent_model <- eval.models(enmeval_results)[[best_settings$tune.args]]

# Project habitat suitability across the study area on the cloglog
# (0-1, probability-like) scale
suitability <- terra::predict(clim_selected, maxent_model, type = "cloglog", na.rm = TRUE)

mapview(suitability) +
  mapview(niph_thinned, col.regions = "purple", cex = 3)
```

### Notes

- Feature class/regularisation multiplier combinations are chosen by lowest AICc - worth sanity-checking against cross-validated AUC and omission rate too, both in `enmeval_results@results`

- Block partitioning splits occurrences into 4 spatial folds by default - given how clustered/narrow-ranged this species is, worth checking the fold sizes are reasonable (`enmeval_results@occs.grp`)

## Evaluate the model

```{r}
# Cross-validated performance of the selected feature class / regularisation
# multiplier, from the spatial block cross-validation done during tuning
best_settings |>
  select(fc, rm, auc.val.avg, auc.val.sd, or.10p.avg, or.mtp.avg, AICc)
```

To use this model for quantifying habitat area, we need to convert the continuous suitability surface into a binary suitable/unsuitable classification. We'll use the threshold that maximises the sum of sensitivity and specificity (maxSSS) across the training presence and background points, which tends to be a more robust choice than a fixed percentile threshold (Liu et al. 2013).

```{r}
# Predicted suitability at presence and background locations
# (na.omit drops any points falling on NA cells at the study area's edge)
pred_occs_raw <- terra::extract(suitability, vect(niph_thinned), ID = FALSE)[[1]]
pred_bg_raw <- terra::extract(suitability, vect(bg_points), ID = FALSE)[[1]]

pred_occs <- na.omit(pred_occs_raw)
pred_bg <- na.omit(pred_bg_raw)

# Flag how many points fell outside the study area mask (see earlier note on
# occurrences sitting outside the study area)
message(sum(is.na(pred_occs_raw)), " of ", length(pred_occs_raw), " presence points dropped (NA cell)")
message(sum(is.na(pred_bg_raw)), " of ", length(pred_bg_raw), " background points dropped (NA cell)")

# Find the threshold maximising sensitivity + specificity
candidate_thresholds <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.001)
tss <- sapply(candidate_thresholds, function(t) {
  sensitivity <- mean(pred_occs >= t)
  specificity <- mean(pred_bg < t)
  sensitivity + specificity - 1
})

suitability_threshold <- candidate_thresholds[which.max(tss)]
suitability_threshold
```

```{r}
# Binary suitable/unsuitable habitat map at that threshold
suitable_habitat <- suitability >= suitability_threshold

mapview(suitable_habitat) +
  mapview(niph_thinned, col.regions = "purple", cex = 3)
```

### Notes

- `or.10p.avg`/`or.mtp.avg` are cross-validated omission rates (10th percentile and minimum training presence) - worth checking these are reasonably low for the selected settings, not just the AICc ranking

- `suitability_threshold` will be reused later to quantify suitable habitat area under current and future climate

## Download future climate projections

We can download future climate projections from WorldClim's CMIP6 downscaled data. As with the current-climate data, we use `cmip6_tile()` rather than `cmip6_world()` so we only download the one 30x30 degree tile covering our study area, rather than a global raster (`cmip6_world()` has no `lon`/`lat` argument - it always fetches the full-extent global GeoTIFF, \~1-6+ GB per GCM/SSP/time combination, which isn't practical here).

Rather than a single climate model, we use a spread of GCMs (Global Climate Models) so we can later assess how much projected habitat change depends on the choice of model. We also use all four SSPs (emissions scenarios) available in WorldClim's CMIP6 data, and three time periods spanning short- to long-term projections.

```{r}
# GCMs chosen to span a range of climate sensitivity (cooler to hotter projections)
future_gcms <- c("MIROC6", "MPI-ESM1-2-HR", "IPSL-CM6A-LR", "ACCESS-CM2")

# All four SSPs (emissions scenarios) available from WorldClim's CMIP6 data:
# SSP1-2.6 (low), SSP2-4.5 (moderate), SSP3-7.0 (high), SSP5-8.5 (very high)
future_ssps <- c("126", "245", "370", "585")

# Near-, mid-, and long-term projections
future_time <- c("2021-2040", "2041-2060", "2061-2080")

future_scenarios <- expand.grid(
  gcm = future_gcms,
  ssp = future_ssps,
  time = future_time,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Download each GCM/SSP/time tile (same tile as the current-climate download
# above), crop to the study area, and subset to the same VIF-selected predictors
future_clim <- pmap(future_scenarios, function(gcm, ssp, time) {
  clim_future_tile <- geodata::cmip6_tile(
    lon = 135,
    lat = -45,
    model = gcm,
    ssp = ssp,
    time = time,
    var = "bio",
    path = here::here("data")
  )

  # cmip6_tile() returns the same 19 bioclim variables, in the same order,
  # as worldclim_tile() above - reuse those names so we can subset by the
  # VIF-selected predictor names
  names(clim_future_tile) <- names(clim)

  crop(clim_future_tile, vect(study_area), mask = TRUE)[[names(clim_selected)]]
})

names(future_clim) <- paste(future_scenarios$gcm, future_scenarios$ssp, future_scenarios$time, sep = "_")

# Spot-check one scenario
mapview(future_clim[[1]]$bio_3)
```

### Notes

- This downloads 48 tiles (4 GCMs x 4 SSPs x 3 time periods) at the same resolution/extent as the current-climate tile, rather than 48 global rasters. Each tile is \~80 MB, so expect \~3.8 GB total (some of this may already be cached from earlier runs)

- Worth double-checking that `names(clim_future_tile) <- names(clim)` is a safe assumption - it relies on both tiles containing the same 19 bioclim variables in the same order, which should hold but hasn't been explicitly verified

- The two \~6 GB `cmip6_world()` files downloaded earlier aren't used by this version of the code and can be deleted if you want to reclaim the disk space

## Project the model onto future scenarios

```{r}
# Project the fitted model onto each future climate scenario, on the same
# cloglog scale as the current-climate prediction, then apply the same
# suitability threshold to get binary suitable/unsuitable habitat
future_suitability <- map(future_clim, \(scenario_clim) {
  terra::predict(scenario_clim, maxent_model, type = "cloglog", na.rm = TRUE)
})

future_suitable_habitat <- map(future_suitability, \(s) s >= suitability_threshold)

# Spot-check one scenario against the current-climate prediction
mapview(suitability, layer.name = "current") +
  mapview(future_suitability[[1]], layer.name = names(future_suitability)[1])
```

### Notes

- `future_suitability` holds the continuous cloglog surface per scenario, and `future_suitable_habitat` the binary version at `suitability_threshold` - both keyed by the same `GCM_SSP_time` names as `future_clim`

- This applies the *current* suitability threshold to future predictions, which is standard practice, but worth being explicit about in the write-up

## Quantify habitat change over time

```{r}
# Area (km^2) of suitable habitat in a binary TRUE/FALSE raster
suitable_area_km2 <- function(habitat_raster) {
  areas <- expanse(habitat_raster, unit = "km", byValue = TRUE)
  suitable <- areas$area[areas$value == 1]
  if (length(suitable) == 0) 0 else suitable
}

current_area_km2 <- suitable_area_km2(suitable_habitat)

# future_scenarios and future_suitable_habitat share the same row order, since
# both were built from the same pmap() call earlier
ssp_labels <- c(
  "126" = "SSP1-2.6", "245" = "SSP2-4.5", "370" = "SSP3-7.0", "585" = "SSP5-8.5"
)

habitat_change <- future_scenarios |>
  mutate(
    area_km2 = map_dbl(future_suitable_habitat, suitable_area_km2),
    current_area_km2 = current_area_km2,
    change_km2 = area_km2 - current_area_km2,
    pct_change = 100 * change_km2 / current_area_km2,
    # Ordered factor so the time periods plot in chronological order
    time = factor(time, levels = c("2021-2040", "2041-2060", "2061-2080"), ordered = TRUE),
    ssp_label = factor(ssp_labels[ssp], levels = ssp_labels)
  )

habitat_change
```

```{r}
ggplot(habitat_change, aes(x = time, y = pct_change, colour = gcm, group = gcm)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ssp_label) +
  labs(
    title = "Projected change in suitable habitat area over time",
    x = "Time period", y = "Change in suitable area (%)", colour = "GCM"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```

### Notes

- `suitable_area_km2()` sums the area of TRUE cells via `terra::expanse()`, which accounts for cell area distortion (relevant since we're in unprojected lon/lat)

- Worth also reporting the *current* suitable area (`current_area_km2`) as its own figure/stat, not just the % change, since that's part of criterion 2b(iii) too

- Each point is still a single time-slice projection, not a continuous trajectory - worth being explicit about that in the write-up rather than implying a smooth trend between the three time periods

- This only compares suitable habitat *area* - a spatial comparison (e.g. where habitat is lost vs. gained, or a centroid shift) would strengthen the "extent" and "quality" parts of the criterion, and might be worth adding
